ISO. SEVERE RISK TODAY FOR PARTS OF OKLAHOMA⚠️⛈️💨a cold front pushing south across the Plains will bring increasing thunderstorm chances late this afternoon and evening, including a risk for a few severe storms across northern Oklahoma.

Storms are expected to initially develop near the front across southern Kansas before spreading south into northern Oklahoma late this afternoon and evening. The overall setup does not favor a widespread or particularly organized severe weather event, but the combination of extreme heat, instability and very dry air beneath the storms could support locally powerful downbursts. Damaging wind gusts will be the primary concern, with some hail also possible.

One thing that stands out is the potential for strong downdrafts. DCAPE values could approach 1,500 J/kg across northern Oklahoma, which would support isolated gusts approaching 70 mph in the strongest storms, but the messy, outflow-dominant storm mode should keep the probability of gusts that strong relatively low, but localized damaging winds are definitely possible.

Not everyone will see severe weather, but scattered storms developing late today could produce pockets of damaging winds across northern Oklahoma, with the threat spreading southward through the evening. Keep an eye on the 3PM-11PM timeframe⚠️⛈️💨

items.author: GulfCoastUpdates
items.text:
61 YEARS AGO — Hurricane #Betsy made landfall in SE #Louisiana near Grand Isle as a Category 4.  

Its track was one of the most unique you will ever see.  It looked like it would curve north away from the Gulf Coast twice, but high pressure built back in both times and forced it westward. 

My parents have told me many stories of this storm.  My dad told me the news said the worst was over and they could go to sleep.  Then he said he was woken up with water rising quickly into his room.  He lived in Arabi at the time. 

Levees breached and several areas including Gentilly, the Upper Ninth Ward, the Lower Ninth Ward as well as Arabi and Chalmette were flooded up to 8 feet of water in spots.  Nearly 164,000 homes were flooded, with about 60,000 people stranded in the city.  Many had to be rescued by boat and helicopter. 

For a generation, Betsy was “the storm” — the one parents and grandparents often referenced.  Betsy was a warning of how vulnerable New Orleans truly was, decades before Katrina would confirm that vulnerability once again.

One year from now, day will turn to night over the land of the pharaohs, for longer than any eclipse in a lifetime.

On August 2, 2027, a total solar eclipse sweeps across southern Spain, North Africa, and the Arabian Peninsula, and near Luxor, Egypt, totality will last up to 6 minutes and 23 seconds. That's extraordinary. Most total eclipses give just two or three minutes. This is the longest totality visible from easily accessible land until the year 2114, earning it the nickname "eclipse of the century."

The path of the Moon's shadow crosses Spain, Morocco, Algeria, Libya, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia. Luxor sits almost dead centre, where the eclipsed Sun will hang nearly overhead at about 82 degrees, and the region offers roughly an 80% chance of clear August skies, among the most reliable anywhere on the path.

⚠️ Certified eclipse glasses are essential except during totality itself. If you can travel to the path, start planning now 🌑☀️

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🌌  For a few nights next week, two galaxies will grace the sky at once, and it may be your last good look at the Milky Way's heart this year.

The New Moon on September 11 brings the darkest skies of the month, with the ideal window running roughly September 8 to 14. With no moonlight to wash out faint light, this is one of the final chances in 2026 for Northern Hemisphere observers to see the glowing core of our own Milky Way before it slips below the horizon until spring.

Just after darkness falls, look low toward the southwest to find the Milky Way's central region in Sagittarius, marked by the Teapot asterism, its "steam" rising toward the galaxy's heart. It's a soft, mottled band of light, the combined glow of billions of stars 26,000 light-years away, threaded with dark dust lanes.

Then turn to the east. Climbing higher each hour, between the Great Square of Pegasus and the W of Cassiopeia, sits the Andromeda Galaxy (M31). At 2.5 million light-years, it's the most distant object visible to the naked eye, a faint oval smudge that becomes an elongated glow through binoculars. The light reaching your eyes left Andromeda before our species existed.

🔭 Get well away from city lights and let your eyes adapt for 20 to 30 minutes. No telescope needed.

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
When you lose someone you love, the quiet moments are often filled with memories. Late last night, during one of those moments, I came across one of the first selfies Mom and I took after she and Dad moved in with us 13 years ago.

She was so happy to be here, and we were just as happy to have them. We built our home with Mom’s needs in mind, making sure it was accessible and comfortable for her. I remember feeling like she and Dad had been given a new lease on life here and thinking how much they were going to enjoy it.

And they did.

In many ways, it was like they were on a permanent vacation. I took them along to so many of the events I was invited to, and before long, they became celebrities. It always made me smile when people recognized them, stopped to say hello or asked how they were doing. They loved it, and so did I.

So many wonderful memories were made over those 13 years. We’ll continue making them with Dad for as long as the good Lord allows, while always holding close the countless memories we were blessed to make with Mom.

It’s been more than six weeks since Mom passed, and I still think about her every single day. There are moments when the sadness hits, but more often now, the pictures and memories bring a smile before they bring a tear. I’m incredibly grateful for that.

I continue to receive heartfelt messages from so many of you sharing your own journeys with grief. Your stories have helped me tremendously, and I hope that by sharing mine, I’ve helped some of you too. As painful and lonely as losing someone can feel, there is great comfort in knowing that others understand, that others have walked this road, and that people genuinely care about your journey.

So, keep taking it one day at a time. There is no timetable for grief and no single “right” way to navigate it. The right way is whatever helps you keep moving forward while still honoring the person you love.

I’m learning that moving forward doesn’t mean leaving Mom behind. She comes with us in the stories we tell, the pictures that make us smile, the lessons she taught us, and all those little moments when a memory suddenly finds its way back.

And as long as those memories are with us, a part of her always will be too.

Miss you, Mom. Always will.
❤️❤️❤️❤️

HEAVY RAIN | Heads up, Tampa Bay! Today's rainfall could be a bit heavier than we're used to. Combine that with the fact that some locations near the coast have received 6"+ of rain in the last several days (while others have missed out completely), & we could be looking at the potential for isolated flash flooding.

The NWS has placed our area under a Level 1 (out of 4) risk of flash flooding today. It's the area in green on the map, from around Tampa Bay down to Southwest Florida. 

The area in green will see the chance of slow-moving pop-ups later this afternoon, starting soon after midday. Then, late this afternoon & evening, a robust east coast sea breeze will arrive in our area. Once it does, I expect a large flare-up of rain & storms where this sea breeze crashes into our west coast sea breeze. The area most likely impacted is somewhere between the coast & I-75. Though this could change east to west by a few miles depending on how afternoon pop-ups set up. 

If you can adjust your plans for today, I would definitely try to get all flexible errands & appointments done before 3pm. I understand that for many, your schedule is what it is & flexibility is not an option. Just be prepared & don't rush. Take your time & try to stick to larger roads over smaller ones to avoid those areas that are more likely to flood. 

For most people today, this will just be a rainy afternoon & evening. I'm just trying to make sure that the few who do run into a little trouble are prepared for it. 

Stay safe!

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🪐 Saturn has grown a giant 10-sided shape around its south pole.

NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope has revealed a huge atmospheric wave encircling Saturn’s southern polar region.

It is being called a decagon because it forms a strange 10-sided pattern in the planet’s clouds.

This is not a solid structure.

It is a wave trapped inside one of Saturn’s powerful jet streams, stretching through multiple layers of the atmosphere.

That makes it even more intriguing.

Saturn is already famous for its north-pole hexagon, a six-sided jet stream pattern that has been visible for more than 40 years.

But Cassini saw no sign of a similar long-lived structure in the south before its mission ended in 2017.

Hubble data now show that the southern decagon was already present by 2023, and it appears to be strengthening.

The pattern is also different from the northern hexagon.

It seems less stable, more mobile and still evolving.

Scientists do not yet know what created it, or how long it will last.

But Saturn has just become even stranger.

The planet with a hexagon now has a decagon too.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Sánchez-Lavega et al., “A decagon wave around Saturn’s south pole”, Science Advances (2026)

The transition begins Thursday as the first disturbance pushes through. Winds will increase east of the Cascades, especially through the Columbia Gorge, Kittitas Valley and north-central Oregon. Gusts of 45+ mph are possible in the more wind-prone areas Thursday afternoon and evening.

The main storm then digs south along the coast Friday night into Saturday before swinging inland across Washington and Oregon. Saturday currently looks like the most active day, with widespread cooler conditions, rain and showers expanding across western Washington and Oregon and eventually into eastern Washington, northern Idaho and central-eastern Oregon. Across western Washington and Oregon, rain chances increase Friday night and become greatest Saturday. West of the Cascades, outside of the foothills and mountains, generally 0.25 inch or less of rain is expected. This includes Seattle and Portland. Farther east, Spokane and the Inland Northwest turn breezy Thursday before cooler, showery weather develops Friday through the weekend. The more widespread precipitation arrives Friday night into Saturday, with moderate rainfall possible in the mountains and lighter amounts across the lower elevations. Embedded thunderstorms could locally boost rain amounts. The areas favored to see the most moisture will be across the Cascades where over half an inch will fall. Above 6,500 feet, snow will fall in the mountains with accumulations above 7,500 feet🌧️🍂

EAST TO WEST RADAR BLOOMS: Local radar sites across the eastern U.S. are lighting up with radar blooms. If you loop the radar, you'll note these blooms appear to be developing from east to west. These are birds being detected by radar, not actual precipitation (in most cases). But why are these blooms propagating westward? The answer? Nightfall. 

As Earth rotates from west to east, nightfall arrives on the east coast hours before the west coast. Birds wait to take off until after dark, aided by the relative protection night provides them. This means you'll see bird blooms on radar along the east coast first, gradually developing westward as sunset arrives and those westward birds then take off. This gives the appearance these radar artifacts are somehow traveling westward, when in fact, it's simply the byproduct of Earth's rotation and birds taking advantage!

LOOK UP TONIGHT | NORTHERN LIGHTS POSSIBLE🌌✨a geomagnetic storm could bring an opportunity to see the aurora across parts of the northern United States tonight into early Wednesday! NOAA’s Space Weather Prediction Center is forecasting periods of G1 to G2 geomagnetic storming as enhanced solar wind and recent solar activity interact with Earth’s magnetic field.

If conditions come together, the best opportunities in the Lower-48 will be across the northern tier, including parts of Washington, Idaho, Montana, North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan. If geomagnetic activity becomes stronger than forecast, the aurora could become visible or photographable somewhat farther south. Farther north, Alaska and much of Canada will have an even better opportunity, with aurora potentially visible across a much larger area where skies are clear and dark.

As always with the Northern Lights, there are no guarantees. The exact intensity and timing can change quickly, while clouds and light pollution will also play a major role. Find a dark location with a clear view toward the northern horizon, and remember that phone cameras can sometimes capture colors that are difficult to see with the naked eye🌌✨

The Climate Prediction Center has issued their tropical outlook today for the remainder of September. 

In the new outlook, the agency suggests that the next tropical system in the Atlantic may form late in the month closer to the United States & the Bahamas.

Each of these has developed from a decaying front. As we move into late Sept & Oct these fronts will become a common occurrence in the SW Atlantic & the Gulf & each will need to be watched for development.

🌡️ The world is now set to cross the 1.5°C global warming limit.

A new UNEP report says global temperature rise is likely to exceed 1.5°C within the next few years.

That does not mean one hot year has broken the Paris Agreement forever.

The 1.5°C limit is judged over long-term warming, not a single calendar year.

But the direction is now clear.

UNEP says even the most optimistic pathway sees warming peak around 1.8°C, while other scenarios go beyond 2°C.

Above 1.5°C, every extra fraction of a degree makes climate impacts more dangerous.

Heatwaves intensify. Wildfires grow. Floods become more destructive. Ecosystems weaken. Low-lying islands and coastal cities face rising risks.

The report says the best remaining path is now “overshoot, peak and decline.”

That means cutting emissions fast enough to keep the overshoot as low and short as possible, adapting to unavoidable damage, and eventually bringing temperatures back down.

Carbon removal will be needed, but it cannot replace deep emissions cuts.

This is not a permission slip to give up on 1.5°C.

It is a warning that the world must now fight to return to it.

📄 REPORT
📌 United Nations Environment Programme, “Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return”, UNEP (2026)

HAWAII | Kauai Island Utility Cooperative update on post-Lowell recovery: 90% of customers without power. This is going to be a long, slow process as debris may be in the way of restoration. 

Full statement: 

"NEWS RELEASE: Hurricane Lowell caused significant damage to Kauaʻi Island Utility Cooperative’s transmission and distribution system as it passed over Kauaʻi overnight, leaving most of the island without power.

Approximately 90% of KIUC members experienced an outage at some point during the storm. As of this morning, approximately 33,000 of KIUC’s 36,000 member accounts remain without power.

KIUC crews began assessing damage this morning. With approximately 1,500 miles of transmission and distribution lines across Kauaʻi, the assessment and restoration effort will be extensive. Road closures, debris and other access limitations may also affect the ability of crews to reach damaged areas.

“Our first priority is making sure conditions are safe for our crews, emergency responders and the public,” said KIUC President and Chief Executive Officer David Bissell. “We know our members want to know when their power will be restored. Right now, we need to understand the extent of the damage and what repairs are necessary before we can provide reliable restoration estimates.”

Before damaged portions of the system can be re-energized, crews must inspect lines and equipment, identify damage and determine what repairs are necessary to safely restore power. As areas are assessed and conditions allow, repair and restoration work will proceed.
KIUC is mobilizing all available resources to restore power as safely and quickly as possible.

Given the extent of the storm damage, members should prepare for outages that may last several days or longer in some areas.

“This will be a significant island-wide restoration effort, and we ask for our members’ patience as our crews work to assess the system and begin repairs,” Bissell said. “We will provide restoration estimates as soon as we have enough information to do so responsibly.”

KIUC expects to provide another update this afternoon based on information gathered during the initial damage assessments.

Members are urged to stay well away from downed power lines and always assume that any downed line is energized. Downed lines and other electrical hazards should be reported to KIUC or emergency authorities.

Updates will be provided through KIUC’s website, social media channels and local news media as additional information becomes available."

While we have seen 5 named tropical storms this year, all of them have been weak and short-lived, with 0 storms reaching hurricane strength. This leads to why Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) matters: ACE is a metric used by meteorologists to measure the total wind energy output of a season by factoring in both the maximum intensity and the duration of every named storm.

Because ACE is calculated by taking the square of a storm's maximum sustained winds every six hours, weak tropical storms that quickly dissipate barely make a dent in the overall seasonal total. Through September 8, the 2026 season has generated an incredibly low ACE of just 4.40, undercutting the previous record low of 4.80 by this point in 1984.

For context on just how historically dormant the Atlantic basin has been, the long-term average ACE through this exact date is 45.91.

COOLER SOUTHERN WINTER | El Niño has been in the headlines for months for all its impacts. One that hasn't materialized yet is a cooler & wetter fall/winter for the southern U.S. 

The EURO monthly outlook shows this well. Though don't get too excited just yet. It's probably at least 6-8 weeks away. 

The maps below show how much above normal (red/orange) or below normal (blues) monthly temps will be across the U.S. 

September across the South looks pretty warm, with cooler-than-normal weather out west. We've definitely seen a lot of heat this month across the MidSouth & Lower Mississippi River Valley. 

The EURO shows that by Oct those "cooler-than-normal" conditions will begin to move east into the South-Central U.S. For the Southeast & Florida, temps in Oct. are still likely to be close to or just above normal. 

It's not until you get into Nov & Dec that the "cooler-than-normal" temps really start to take over the Southeast & Florida. This should also strengthen into January & February. 

The culprit? Rain! We'll see more rain events than normal, more fronts, more clouds & that should NUDGE temperatures lower. 

Just remember, we're talking about the AVERAGE over a whole month. Every day will NOT be cold. There will be normal days & there will be some warm or even hot days too. It's when you look at the month as a whole that you'll see the averages work out to be somewhat below normal.

Hang in there! Cooler weather is on the way.

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🐋 Whale calls have revealed a strange echo of Einstein’s relativity.

Scientists studying how whale sounds travel underwater have found an unexpected wave effect that can make sound appear to outrun its normal speed limit.

Whales are often tracked using hydrophones, underwater microphones that compare when a call reaches different receivers.

But if a whale is close to the ocean surface, its call does not take just one path.

Some sound travels directly to the receiver. Some bounces off the surface first.

When those two paths meet, they can interfere with each other and shift the strongest peak of the signal earlier than expected.

That can make the wave packet seem to move faster than sound in seawater, which is usually about 1,500 meters per second.

In simulations, some apparent speeds reached around 3,000 meters per second.

But this does not break physics.

The information carried by the wave still stays within the true speed limit. Only the peak of the combined signal appears to jump ahead.

That is the Einstein connection.

Special relativity allows wave shapes to behave strangely, but it does not allow information to outrun light.

A whale call may have exposed a subtle trick of waves, and it could make future whale tracking far more accurate.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Spiesberger et al., “Supersonic and superluminal energy and speed of information via temporal interference in a dispersionless environment”, Physical Review E (2026)

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
RECORD-SETTING QUIET HURRICANE SEASON...SO FAR

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has been remarkably quiet, with just five named storms and still no hurricanes. The well-advertised, historic El Niño has certainly helped put the brakes on tropical activity.

Just how quiet has it been? Through September 8, this season has produced the lowest Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) of any Atlantic season since 1950.

ACE measures how active a hurricane season is by factoring in both storm strength and how long storms last. The stronger and longer-lived the storms, the higher the ACE.

This year’s ACE through September 8 is a measly 4.4. For some perspective, in 1995 it had already reached a whopping 148.5 by this same point!

And another record may be just around the corner. It’s looking increasingly likely we’ll make it past September 11 without a hurricane, which would make 2026 the latest on record for the Atlantic’s first hurricane.

There’s still plenty of hurricane season left, of course, but with all the weather hype and doom-and-gloom these days, it’s nice to talk about a good weather record for a change!

🔴WARNING: A tornado has been detected by radar, or spotted by a chaser/EMS/spotter. Seek shelter!

The same applies for severe thunderstorms as well!

items.text:
Hurricane Lowell is bringing heavy rain, strong winds and even a tornado threat to Hawaii’s western islands.

It’s the second hurricane to impact Hawaii this season, following Hurricane Lala in mid-August.

Meanwhile, here in the Atlantic, we still haven’t had our first hurricane of the season, and I’m perfectly fine keeping it that way! 

You may have noticed that both hurricanes to impact Hawaii start with the letter “L”. The two “L” storms are just a coincidence. Lala formed in the Central Pacific, where storms use a separate, continuous list of Hawaiian names that doesn’t restart each year. Lowell formed in the Eastern Pacific, where storms use the traditional alphabetical naming system. Two different basins, two different naming systems, both just happened to give us an “L” storm.
🌀🌀

MID-MONTH MOISTURE SIGNAL FOR THE SOUTHWEST & SOUTHERN PLAINS🌵🌧️⛈️there continues to be an encouraging signal for increased moisture and precipitation across a large part of the Southwest and eventually the Southern Plains heading into mid-September!

The latest 6-10 day outlook for September 13-17 favors above-normal precipitation across Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, Colorado and much of the Great Plains, including West Texas, North Texas and Oklahoma. This is due to a persistent trough near the West Coast combined with the broader upper-level pattern should favor increased precipitation from the Southwest through the Rockies and into much of the Plains.

The wetter signal continues in the 8-14 day period, September 15-21. Above-normal precipitation is favored across much of the West, while Oklahoma and essentially all of Texas are also favored to see above-normal precipitation. Kansas and Nebraska remain on the wetter side of the outlook as well.

For the Southwest, the pattern could become particularly active. Southerly flow may help transport deeper moisture northward, with the potential for a surge of Gulf of California moisture. There is currently a risk for heavy precipitation across parts of the Desert Southwest and Great Basin from September 15-19, along with a risk of flooding.

While it won't rain every day or everywhere, the broader trend is for increasing moisture and more opportunities for precipitation from the Southwest into parts of the Southern Plains during the middle and latter part of September🌵🌧️⛈️

DESTRUCTIVE HURRICANE-FORCE GUSTS ⚠️ possible across parts of Kauaʻi and Niʻihau tonight! Hurricane Lowell is tracking toward Hawaii and beginning to interact with an upper-level low. As this interaction occurs, Lowell’s wind field is becoming larger and increasingly asymmetric, with the strongest winds extending well east of the center - toward Hawaii.

Hurricane-force sustained winds now extend as far as 60 miles from the center, while tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 175 miles. This is especially concerning for Kauaʻi and Niʻihau, which will be on the more impactful side of the hurricane as Lowell makes its closest approach tonight. The core of Lowell is forecast to pass near or just west of Niʻihau tonight into early Tuesday.

Lowell currently has sustained winds of 110 mph with gusts to 130 mph and is moving north-northeast at a fast 17 mph. Hurricane conditions are expected across Kauaʻi beginning this afternoon or evening, and winds over and around the islands’ mountainous terrain can be up to 30% stronger than near-surface winds, especially in exposed locations.

The exact track of the eye is not the only concern. Lowell’s expanding wind field means damaging winds could extend well away from the center, increasing the potential for significant impacts across Kauaʻi and Niʻihau tonight⚠️

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
ANOTHER EARLY-SEASON STORM SYSTEM COULD BRING WEATHER CHANGES TO THE NORTHWEST THIS WEEKEND BUT THERE ARE QUESTION🌧️❄️💨⛈️ confidence continues to increase that an upper-level trough will drop south out of British Columbia late Friday into the weekend, bringing the potential for a fall-like pattern change to parts of the Pacific and Inland Northwest, and eventually the Northern U.S. Rockies.

There are questions on how widespread rain will be but showers should become increasingly likely across Washington and into northern Oregon and Idaho. The best opportunity for a wetter period currently favors Washington and northern Idaho, while precipitation could become more limited farther south but it depends on how deep the storm system becomes and how far north or south it tracks. A few thunderstorms may accompany the system across parts of northeast Washington and northern Idaho as colder air aloft moves overhead.

The trough will send much cooler air south across the Northwest, with the cooling eventually reaching northern California and the Sierra. This comes after a significant midweek warm-up, so the change could be especially noticeable. Breezy to locally gusty winds are also expected as the system moves through.

Colder air could should lower snow levels down to 6,000-7,000 feet in Washington and Oregon and 7,000-8,000 feet across parts of Idaho and the Northern U.S. Rockies, allowing some of the highest peaks to pick up accumulating snow. It's uncertain how much snow Washington and Oregon see but there's higher confidence in snow from Idaho into Montana and Wyoming.

There is still high uncertainty regarding exactly how deep and far south this system digs. A deeper-slower storm would support more widespread rain, colder temperatures and greater mountain snow potential. A farther north or east track would keep precipitation more limited, particularly across Oregon and northern California🌧️❄️💨⛈️

The biggest concern is that the forecast track has shifted east, closer to Hawaii. The center is now expected to pass near or just west of Niihau tonight into early Tuesday. Kauai County is under a Hurricane Warning, and Oahu has now been upgraded to a Tropical Storm Warning. Conditions will deteriorate this afternoon and evening. 

Lowell should gradually weaken but is forecast to remain a hurricane while passing the western Hawaiian Islands. The official forecast has it near 110 mph tonight, around 100 mph early Tuesday, then weakening more rapidly Tuesday night and Wednesday as wind shear increases and the hurricane encounters cooler water. 

Kauai could receive 6 to 10 inches of additional rainfall with isolated totals up to 16 inches. Oahu and Maui County could see 4 to 8 inches with isolated 10 inch amounts. Significant flash flooding and mudslides are possible. A 2 to 4 foot storm surge is possible in Kauai County, particularly along southern Kauai and Niihau, accompanied by large destructive waves. Several tornadoes are also possible near Kauai and Niihau.

HURRICANE LOWELL | SEPT 7 2026 7 AM HST

Lowell is the PERFECT example of why looking at the forecast cone will give you the wrong idea of what to expect. 

The forecast cone only covers where the eye of the hurricane goes 66% of the time. A hurricane is MUCH larger than the eye. 

In Lowell, when it's passing Hawaii, the cone only extends about 40 miles east & west of the exact forecast path. Looking at the cone looks like a miss. 

But Lowell is a BIG hurricane & its winds will spread out farther as it weakens & heads north.

When the storm is passing Hawaii, hurricane winds will extend 60 miles east of the center, about 20 miles outside of the cone. 

Strong tropical storm winds (58-73 mph) will extend over 100 miles east of the center into Kauai County.

Weaker tropical storm winds of 40-57 mph will extend out to 180 miles east of the center into O'ahu. 

Hurricanes are MUCH more than their center (the eye). Don't focus on the cone. Focus well beyond the cone to see if you're going to be impacted & how.

Even Hilo on the Big Island, over 300 miles from the center, may see flooding rains from this system.

HAWAII HURRICANE WARNING‼️🚨🌀a Hurricane Warning is now in effect for Kauaʻi and Niʻihau as Hurricane Lowell’s forecast track has shifted east, bringing the powerful storm closer to the western Hawaiian Islands! A Tropical Storm Watch is also in effect for Oʻahu.

Lowell remains a Category 3 hurricane with sustained winds of 115 mph, moving north-northeast at 14 mph. The center is forecast to pass just west of Kauaʻi County late today into early Tuesday, but even a small additional shift east or west could significantly change the impacts. Hurricane-force winds are now possible on Kauaʻi and Niʻihau, with tropical-storm-force winds potentially reaching Oʻahu.

Heavy rain and thunderstorms will affect the entire state through Tuesday and could linger into Wednesday. The Honolulu NWS projects 6-10 inches of additional rain on Kauaʻi, with isolated totals up to 16 inches. Oʻahu and Maui County could receive 4-8 inches with isolated totals near 10 inches, while the Big Island could see isolated amounts up to 12 inches. Significant flash flooding, landslides and road closures are possible, especially on Kauaʻi and across southern and eastern portions of the Big Island.

Rapidly building surf will create another serious threat. South-facing shores of Kauaʻi could see waves reach 20-30 feet this afternoon, while damaging surf, coastal flooding and erosion may affect Kauaʻi and possibly Oʻahu as the swell peaks near high tide. Coastal roads and infrastructure could be damaged.

Lowell’s outer rainbands may also produce short-lived tornadoes or waterspouts, primarily around Kauaʻi and Niʻihau Monday into Monday night. Conditions should gradually improve Tuesday as Lowell moves north, but residents should complete preparations immediately and remain alert for rapidly changing warnings‼️🌀
